blocker.summary: r440 decompiled sub_821D6C20/sub_821D7DE0 and found sub_821D7DE0 is the game's main-loop entry, calling sub_821D5F48 then sub_821D6C20 as two 'must succeed' init steps right before an infinite game loop; sub_821D6C20 dereferences the null global at 0x82935D98 completely unguarded as its literal first action (the known crash site), and its success-path body reads indexed settings/resource values into that object's vtable -- textbook GPU/renderer device configuration. r441 decompiled sub_821D5F48 itself (new tool, scripts/DecompileD5F48SettingsHelpers.java, committed): confirms it is unambiguously the Xenos/renderer bootstrap (hardcoded 1280x720 resolution, MiB-scale buffer sizes). More importantly, r441 found and then live-verified the actual writer of 0x82935D98: ppc_recomp.23.cpp:20257 has 'addi r11,r11,23960' + 'stw r3,0(r11)' -- a real store to that exact address, present in r436/r439's own '23960' grep results all along but misclassified as another load on a too-quick read (self-corrected here). A live gdb breakpoint at the exact host instruction (0x555555724df8, confirmed within sub_821D5F48's true compiled bounds) never fires -- the process goes straight from sub_821D5F48 to the known sub_821D6C20 crash without ever reaching it. This fully reconciles with r437's watchpoint proof: the writer code is real retail code, but sub_821D5F48 returns via a different, earlier return path (among several nested ones seen in the decompilation) in this run, one that never reaches the write block while still returning success to its caller. The real divergence from real hardware is whichever condition selects that earlier return, not the write block itself. Named for r442: live-trace which return path sub_821D5F48 actually takes and what condition selects it. The native_vulkan_backend.cpp backlog commit decision (r433/r434/r438) remains the other open, user-dependent thread.
